name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Wednesday 9 January 1991 (English cryptic)

clue.text: Joseph and his brother dramatically champions of wind and wave?

blocks.note: first meaning: Joseph and Charles, the two brothers in Sheridan's play The School for Scandal, share this surname, pluralised
second meaning: read as two words, ..., experts at riding the sea

explanation.surface: A biblical-sounding Joseph and his brother are cast as heroic battlers against storm and sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joseph and his brother' points at the Bible, but 'dramatically' sends you to the stage: Joseph Surface and his brother Charles in The School for Scandal. Split the answer as SURF ACES for the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Surface brothers are a pair of Sheridan characters, and surf aces are top surfers, masters of breakers driven by the wind.

clue.text: Go away or I'll t!

blocks.note: surface reading: a shouted order to clear off
setter's reading: a threat whose last word is missing all but its final letter, so the answer is the part left out

explanation.walkthrough: The OCR shows '1', which would point at 1 Down, but that makes no sense; a printed 't' does: the answer plus t completes the threat.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an interjection used to drive off animals or people, telling them to leave at once.

clue.text: Language spoken by dove?

indicators.note: something spoken is heard rather than read, so the bird's name is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a dove is a kind of pigeon

explanation.surface: A question about what tongue a dove might talk in.
explanation.definitionFit: A pidgin is a simplified contact tongue that grows up between speakers who share no common one.

clue.text: 7 and 9, headless, make capital people

indicators.note: something headless has lost its top, so the opening letter of the second number is dropped
to make here is to build something new out of the materials, so the letters are put together in another order

blocks.note: the number written as a word
the number nine written as a word, without its first letter

explanation.surface: A cross-reference clue claiming entries 7 and 9, cut short, combine to name a city's people.
explanation.walkthrough: '7 and 9' looks like a pointer to 7 Across and 9 Across, but it means the numbers themselves, spelt out; only nine loses its head here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Viennese are the inhabitants of Vienna, the capital city of Austria.

clue.text: A measure in the factory or a sound in the monastery

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the measure goes within the word for the works

blocks.note: taken as written
an inch is a unit of length
a plant is an industrial works

explanation.surface: Two contrasting workplaces: a measuring task on the factory floor, and something heard in a cloister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A measure in the factory' reads like one idea, a work quota perhaps, but it is three pieces: the measure sits inside the factory, and 'or' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainchant is the unaccompanied single-line singing of the medieval church, still heard from monks at their services.

clue.text: Hoodoo on radio opera tor in abbey town

blocks.note: a hoodoo is a jinx or curse, as is a hex
an amateur radio operator is a ham; the OCR splits 'operator'

explanation.surface: A curse carried on the airwaves by a radio operator somewhere in an old abbey town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' just places the second piece after the first, read as 'radio operator'. HEXHAM is a market town in Northumberland, England, built around its abbey.
explanation.definitionFit: Hexham grew up around the priory church founded by St Wilfrid, still known as Hexham Abbey.

clue.text: Danger of dry land? If otherwise, play on word "Horrific"

blocks.note: surface reading: a hazard facing parched country in an Australian summer
setter's reading: the clue admits to being a pun, with 'if' turned the other way round making the start of the second word

explanation.walkthrough: In January 1991 this works two ways: the menace of the dry Australian bush in summer, and the US president's firepower aimed at the desert of the Gulf. Only the reversed 'if' of the tail is clear.
explanation.definitionFit: A bushfire is a wildfire in scrub or forest, the great seasonal hazard of dry Australian country.

clue.text: Hitherto, place of divorce between couple that never meet

indicators.note: something between two things is flanked by them, so the city goes inside the pair

blocks.note: east and west, opposite compass points that never meet; this is the first
Reno, Nevada, was famous for quick divorces
the second of the pair, west

explanation.surface: A couple who never see each other have, until now, been visiting a divorce town.
explanation.walkthrough: The couple sounds like an estranged pair of people, but it is East and West, which 'never the twain shall meet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ere now is an old-fashioned phrase meaning before this time, the same as hitherto or until now.

clue.text: Oberon and Titania, moonlighting, were with me, it doesn't say for how long

blocks.note: surface reading: the fairy king and queen working a second job by night

blocks.clueFragment: with me, it doesn't say for how long
blocks.note: setter's reading: Oberon greets Titania in A Midsummer Night's Dream with a famous line about an unlucky moonlit meeting; the clue quotes it, leaving out the moonlight

explanation.walkthrough: In A Midsummer Night's Dream Oberon greets Titania with 'Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania', so by moonlight they were badly met; the rest of the clue is padding whose wordplay is not clear.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people who are ill met encounter each other unluckily or with hostility, as the quarrelling fairy rulers do.

clue.text: Parched condition in Paris, in that case

blocks.note: soif is the French word for thirst

explanation.surface: Someone in Paris discussing what happens when you are thirsty.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the French word into its two halves and swap them; no word in the clue signals the swap.
explanation.definitionFit: If so is a conditional phrase meaning provided that is true, the same as in that case.

clue.text: Go-ahead for eau-de-Nil?

blocks.note: first meaning: permission to proceed, the signal at a crossing
second meaning: eau-de-Nil is a pale, light green colour, so it is literally a light green

explanation.walkthrough: Eau-de-Nil, 'Nile water' in French, sounds like a drink but is the name of a pale green shade; the question mark flags the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A green light is both a signal to go and, read literally, a pale shade of green such as eau-de-Nil.

clue.text: Comer on stage, crazy on point

blocks.note: surface reading: someone making an entrance in a play
setter's reading: the definition is the last word, sharpness of mind; how the opening words build the answer is not clear from the printed clue

explanation.walkthrough: The first part may play on 'a cue man', an actor who comes on at his cue, but 'crazy' has no clear role, so treat this parse as uncertain; the crossings fix the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Acumen is keenness of judgement, a mind with a sharp point to it, from the Latin for sharpness.

clue.text: We want Holm to set . blades at blades

indicators.note: to set is to put in order or arrange, so these letters are laid out afresh

blocks.note: the three words as letters

explanation.surface: A demand that someone called Holm be put to work, with talk of blades.
explanation.walkthrough: The full stop in the copy is a stray mark. The definition plays on two kinds of blade: a mower's cutters set to work on blades of grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Mowing the lawn means running cutting blades over the grass, whose leaves are also called blades.

clue.text: We shall one day give an impression or cross to our side

indicators.note: or offers the alternative arrangement, so the two words of the phrase trade places

blocks.clueFragment: give an impression or cross to our side
blocks.note: to come over is both to give an impression (he comes over as shy) and to cross to our side

explanation.surface: A hopeful crowd promises future triumph, or invites someone to defect to their camp.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a fill-in: the anthem 'We shall overcome some day' with the missing word left as a gap. The phrasal verb that the rest defines has its halves swapped.
explanation.definitionFit: The civil-rights anthem promises 'We shall overcome some day'; the gap is the verb meaning defeat or prevail over.

clue.text: Avoid saying it has a serrated ovipositor

blocks.note: a saw is an old saying or proverb
to fly from something is to flee or avoid it

explanation.surface: Someone shying away from mentioning an insect's saw-edged egg-laying tube.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the opposite order to the clue. The definition is fair because the insect's toothed egg-laying organ is what gives it its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawflies are wasp relatives whose females cut into plants with a toothed, saw-like ovipositor to lay eggs.

clue.text: Power of movement means a number always get older

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty
ever means always
to age is to grow older

explanation.surface: A rule that a number of people are always growing older, presented as a law of motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Leverage is the mechanical advantage a lever gives, the extra power to move a load.

clue.text: Ozone to the rescue in . World War II

blocks.clueFragment: to the rescue in . World War II
blocks.note: the wartime Air-Sea Rescue service picked up airmen downed at sea

explanation.surface: Ozone arrives to save the day during the Second World War.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words of the wartime service's name are taken in the other order; the full stop is a stray mark in the copy. Ozone is a jokey everyday name for bracing seaside air.
explanation.definitionFit: Popular usage calls the fresh, tangy smell of the seaside ozone, though it is really just air off the sea.

clue.text: Decree about epitaph in its first word?

blocks.note: re means concerning or about
writing that holds the letters RIP, the usual opening of an epitaph

explanation.surface: A legal order concerning a grave inscription, asking what its opening word should be.
explanation.walkthrough: RIP, short for Requiescat in pace, opens many epitaphs and sits inside the second piece; exactly how 'its first word' reads is uncertain, but the crossings fix the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rescript is a formal written decree or edict, originally a Roman emperor's or pope's written ruling.

clue.text: Sci-fi writer in love with Mavis?

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, written O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A science-fiction author is said to be in love with a woman named Mavis.
explanation.walkthrough: No word signals the rearrangement; the question mark admits the liberty. Isaac Asimov wrote the Foundation and robot stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Asimov was one of the best-known science-fiction authors of the twentieth century, writer of I, Robot.

clue.text: Saint Joan's place has a head start in the records

indicators.note: a head start is a lead at the very front, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: Joan of Arc
the word has supplies only its opening letter
St Ives, the Cornish seaside town named after a saint
padding that tells you the saint stands for a town

explanation.surface: The birthplace of the saint gets an early mention in the historical documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint Joan's place' reads as one phrase but splits: the saint's place is St Ives, a town in Cornwall, England, and Joan's is the Arc of her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Archives are collections of historical records, and the place where such documents are kept.

clue.text: Fugitive drops article in airfield

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it fall away, so the little word goes missing

blocks.note: a fugitive is one who has run off
a is the indefinite article, the letter taken out

explanation.surface: An escaped prisoner abandons a newspaper piece somewhere on an aerodrome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a newspaper story but is the grammatical article. The definition stretches a little: the strip is part of an airfield rather than the whole of one.
explanation.definitionFit: A runway is the paved strip on an aerodrome where aircraft take off and land.

clue.text: 'Ere's cannabis: cannabis is an alkali

indicators.note: the dropped aitch of a Cockney 'here's' tells you to treat the next word the same way, losing its opening letter

blocks.note: pot is slang for cannabis
hash, short for hashish, is another name for the drug; it loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A street dealer offers drugs, then a pedant declares cannabis to be a chemical alkali.
explanation.walkthrough: Two different slang words for the same drug; the h-less 'ere's shows the second is said Cockney-style, 'ash.
explanation.definitionFit: Potash is potassium carbonate or a related compound, a strongly alkaline salt once made from wood ashes.

clue.text: Model task, impressive if I'm on top of it

indicators.note: the answer becomes the longer word once these two letters are placed above it, so the clue builds the answer by taking them off

blocks.note: impressive means grand or imposing
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: An ambitious modelling assignment would be impressive if the speaker were in charge of it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on top of' means at the start, so the longer word is I'M placed over the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Posing, holding still in positions for a photographer or artist, is the core of a model's work.

clue.text: Negro who told stories about United Nations in force

blocks.note: re means concerning or about
UN is the standard abbreviation
muscle means power or force

explanation.surface: A storyteller is described in the dated language of 1991 as telling tales about the UN in power.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of the three pieces are rearranged, though no word in the clue signals it. Uncle Remus is the elderly Black narrator of Joel Chandler Harris's Brer Rabbit stories; the clue's wording is of its time.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Remus narrates Joel Chandler Harris's collected African-American folk tales, such as the Brer Rabbit stories.

clue.text: Legal term relating to check

blocks.note: to rein in is to check or restrain

explanation.surface: A lawyer's term connected with checking.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the four-letter word into two halves and swap them; nothing in the clue signals the swap.
explanation.definitionFit: In re is Latin used in legal titles, meaning in the matter of, that is, concerning or relating to.

clue.text: Devil first gets Zulu warriors

blocks.note: an imp is a little devil
I is the Roman numeral one, as in first

explanation.surface: The devil takes the lead and captures a band of Zulu fighters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devil first' reads as an instruction to put the devil at the front, but 'first' supplies the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An impi is a Zulu regiment or armed band of warriors, the word also used in the plural sense.

clue.text: Insect with garments worn in Mayfair?

blocks.note: surface reading: a creepy-crawly dressed up in clothes
setter's reading: the answer splits into a body part and a hairpiece, the sort of thing worn in a smart district

explanation.walkthrough: Mayfair is an expensive district of London. The second half of the answer is a hairpiece; how the clue gets the first half is not clear, but the crossings fix the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An earwig is a small insect with pincers at the tail end, once believed to crawl into ears.

clue.text: Dickens hero happening to let gas escape

blocks.note: an event is a happening; its first letter moves to the end
Pip is the hero of Great Expectations

explanation.surface: A Dickensian hero's adventure, apparently ending in some flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: The hero is placed inside the happening after its opening letter has moved to the back; nothing signals either step, so this is the loosest clue in the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A vent-pipe is a pipe that lets gas or air escape from a drain, tank or soil stack.
